idiom_name: Exposed Table objects with typed column definitions
implementation_notes: The metadata store is a Kotlin object extending Table: each column is a property built by a typed factory (integer("id"), varchar("name", 64), bool("completed").default(false)) and the table name is the constructor argument, so the declaration is ordinary code the compiler can check. Exposed is reader and engine - queries are written against those column properties and the DSL renders the SQL, and SchemaUtils can create the DDL from the same definitions - so no hand-written row mapper exists. When the persistence model must be declared with annotations instead, Room (compile-time checked, Android) or Jakarta Persistence are the Kotlin-side alternatives.
pitfalls: Table objects are singletons holding the column definitions: defining the same table twice (for example per test) conflicts, and the property names are part of the mapping contract queries rely on.
A missing explicit table name makes Exposed derive one from the object name, which usually does not match the schema.
Column types are resolved per database profile, so switching databases can change the emitted DDL without any change to the table object.

variants.name: Android Room entities (@Entity/@ColumnInfo)
variants.implementation_notes: On Android the metadata store is the annotation set on a data class: @Entity(tableName = "users") with @PrimaryKey, @ColumnInfo(name = "first_name") to rename a column, @Ignore and the indices/ignoredColumns properties. The reader is Room's annotation processor (KSP), which validates the mapping at compile time and generates the DAO implementations and the schema description; the engine is the generated code over SQLite. That buys compile-time checking reflection-based mappers cannot offer, at the cost of a build step and of keeping raw @Query SQL strings in step with the same metadata.
pitfalls: The generated schema hash is versioned: renaming a column without a migration or a destructive fallback makes the database fail to open at runtime.
@Query SQL is checked against the entity metadata only for schema-visible mistakes; a projection that no longer matches the metadata can still compile and fail at run time.

variants.name: Kotlin entities with Jakarta Persistence annotations
variants.idiom_name: @Entity/@Column Kotlin classes on the JPA metamodel
variants.implementation_notes: The JPA path reuses the annotation metadata (@Entity, @Column(name = ...)) on Kotlin classes, but the class must be made proxyable and instantiable: the kotlin-jpa no-arg plugin and the all-open plugin generate the no-argument constructor and open members the provider requires, and var rather than val properties are needed for dirty checking. The metamodel and engine are the provider's, so the mapping knowledge is identical to the Java case; choose it when the stack is already JPA and Kotlin syntax is wanted, and prefer Exposed or Room when the persistence layer is still open.
pitfalls: Without the no-arg and all-open plugins the provider cannot instantiate or proxy the entity, and the failure appears at run time although its cause is build configuration.
val properties and data classes break dirty checking and generated equals/hashCode, so entities usually give up data-class convenience.
